item.title: Commanders roster news: Two signed to practice squad; Vet QB gets workout
item.description: Commanders make several moves as injuries continue to mount
item.content:encoded:
The Washington Commanders had two players from their practice squad poached this week. Unrafted free agent RB Robert Henry Jr. signed with the Seahawks, and veteran CB Terell Smith was signed by the Steelers. The Commanders roster was expected to have a few changes with WR/KR Jaylin Lane going to injured reserve after suffering a serious ankle dislocation and Marcus Mariota reinjuring his MCL.

The Commanders worked out QB Jake Plummer this morning per NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo. He noted that the tream isn’t placing Mariota on IR, and said they weren’t planning on signing Plummer. He’s an option if needed later in the season. Mariota originally sprained his MCL in the first preseason game against the Dolphins. He didn’t play again until Jayden Daniels was injured in Week 2. The team has their bye in Week 7 giving them additional time for Mariota to return without needing to use an IR designation.

Washington also announced two roster moves to fill the two open spots on their practice squad. OLB T.J. Maguranyanga has been with the team as their International Pathways Program player, but Washington used that roster exemption for DT Jeffrey M’ba this year. Now he returns as a regular member of the practice squad, signing today along with S Darren Hall.

The Commanders are also signing WR Nick DeGennaro to the practice squad per ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler. This move isn’t official, and the team will need to make another roster move to open up a spot.

item.title: Fantasy Football: Revisiting preseason expectations after one month of the 2026 season
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen looks back at some August notes to see where things stand today.
item.content:encoded:
Doing projects with my wife is an experience. We’ve been married for almost 20 years, and for about 19 of them, I could’ve sworn we thought the same way. There were signs, though. 

We redid our guest bathroom in 2018 and spent two hours looking at shades of paint. Don’t get me wrong. That had to happen. But debating “Aqua Fiesta” versus “Tropical Sea” as I’m replumbing the shower caught me off guard. But to be fair, her ability to hop into the weeds while keeping a full view of the forest is why we work well together. 

It’d make her a good fantasy football manager, too. We watch games, go to the film or our stat providers and project ahead. But keeping sight of the big picture is key. Four weeks in, it's easy to get lost in the weeds. So, let's step back, revisit a few preseason narratives and see what the forest looks like now.

We Were (Mostly) Right In August

Over the spring and summer, I take a high-level view of ADP data by checking which teams the market wants us to buy. My focus is specifically on the early rounds.

Think about it this way. I went back over the last five years to calculate top-12 hit rates for players by their ADP. You’d assume a more expensive player would net us higher output. And typically you’d be right! Even if we’re dealing with smaller samples at QB and TE, the draft community has a good idea of how to value players. But more broadly, it gives us an idea of what we think about each offense. I’ll use this year’s board as an example.

  • Bears: 5 (players drafted inside the top 72)

  • Bengals: 4

  • Lions: 4

  • Cowboys: 4

On draft day, all we see is names. The adage is “get your guy,” not “get your team.” Sure, we give consideration to their environment. But that’s already part of the cost. And once again, we were kind of cooking when setting prices.

  • Yards per Game: 1st (CHI rank), 11th (CIN rank), 6th (DET rank), 12th (DAL rank)

  • EPA per Drive: 8th, 12th, 4th, 2nd 

  • Team PPR PPG: 8th, 7th, 1st, 4th 

With top-12 marks overall, the production pie for each team has been large enough for everyone to eat. But a few have been left out. Luckily, Colston Loveland is showing signs of life. The same might be the case for a couple of others from this group of teams. 

Burrow changes the protection against the Jaguars double mug. Can see Chase Brown start to step up into the A gap but Burrow stops him. Instead of their usual protection Burrow lets the free runner threw and throws it to Brown in the vacated middle of the field. pic.twitter.com/olIb1jtMbP

— mike (@bengals_sans) October 5, 2026

Credit to the Jaguars’ run defense. They forced Cincinnati into a pass-only script by bottling up the run game. Chase Brown averaged 0.56 adjusted yards before contact per attempt and an 11.1% rushing success rate. And it felt like that all game. But it didn’t stop Brown from staying involved in the offense.

  • Route Rate: 64% (Week 4), 52% (Weeks 1-3)

  • Targets per Route Run: 30%, 19%

  • Target Share: 21%, 11%

Samaje Perine didn’t take over. Instead, we got more of Brown as a receiver, setting a new career-high with 11 receptions. OC Dan Pitcher called their run-game strategy “unsustainable” after just 23 yards on the ground. And as they turn it around, Brown’s totes should turn into touchdowns.

I could make the same case for a receiver in a similar situation.

Just when I thought I couldn’t love Jameson Williams more…

HE HITS THE DAB AFTER A FIRST DOWN IN CAROLINA!!! pic.twitter.com/AbwvsrXk5D

— Max Loeb (@loebsleads) October 5, 2026

The offseason thought of Detroit’s defense turning the Lions into the 2025 Bengals has worked for everyone except Jameson Williams. It took him until Sunday night to crack the top 24. But a quick look under the hood highlights the root cause.

  • Target Rate on In-breaking Routes: 47.1% (2025), 16.0% (2026)

  • Target Rate on Out-breaking Routes: 12.7%, 44.0%

On top of the drops, Williams YAC per reception is down from last season. But when most of his routes are now going to the boundary, even without a significant change in depth, the chance for explosives diminishes. Plus, the time to adjust to a role change increases.

In both cases, our priors about the environment were correct. However, the results don’t add up. Accordingly, isolating the usage metrics that matter, like a 51% air yard share for George Pickens in Week 4, should be our approach before deciding a player isn’t living up to preseason expectations.

Trust Usage Over Points at Tight End

I feel like Charlie Brown in the Lucy-with-the-football meme regarding drafting TEs. Every year it’s the same thing. And there’s no middle ground.

“Tight end is deep this year!”

“If you don’t get the elite guys, just wait until the end of your draft.”

“All I want is a set-it-and-forget-it TE. Get your guy in the early rounds!”

Despite us needing multiple RBs and WRs every week, we’ve built entire team-building strategies around the onesies. Let’s check in with the folks that took the expensive options.

Kirk Cousins with a strike to Michael Mayer for their first TD of the game 🎯@LVvsNO on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/UiGpkm2qRG

— NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026

Wait, that isn’t Brock Bowers.

Of course, we couldn’t start the season without some drama. But losing our second-round TE to start the season was the scenario drafters couldn’t afford. That pick seemingly went up in smoke. And even if you picked up Michael Mayer, you got TE19 and TE25 finishes as emotional compensation. OK, injury situations are impossible to predict. But we got hit with role changes, too.

Colston Loveland with the best celebration of all time for a 5 yard reception that was short of the end zone pic.twitter.com/65DVWbqRXF

— NFL Numbers Guy (@NFLNumbersGuy) September 29, 2026

Colston Loveland had nine targets in all of September and one of the best-coordinated TD cellys … that turned out to be for nothing. Tucker Kraft is averaging 37 YPG. The 2026 draft top 12 feels underwhelming, but it’s not that bad. 

Outside of the obvious, if you took a TE1, you’ve got one by total points. But the weekly results have been frustrating. Bowers (yes, the same guy), Kincaid, Warren and Kittle are the only ones with consecutive top-10 performances. That inconsistency is why Isaiah Likely, Juwan Johnson, T.J. Hockenson and Mike Gesicki have slid into the top 12. But there are a couple of takeaways here.

First, I put together a composite profile of a high-end starter using the eight hits from the TE1 ranks.

  • (Average) Route Rate: 80.8%

  • Targets per Route Run: 23.5%

  • Slot Snap Rate: 29.4%

Think of those numbers above as benchmarks. If your guy is close to at least two of these, you’re in the right neighborhood. Plus, hope flickers for Kraft (70%-plus route rate since W2, 21% TPRR) and Loveland (76% route rate, 35% TPRR in W4). But if I relax those thresholds a little, look who bubbles to the top.

  • Dalton Schultz: TE1 in W2

  • Mark Andrews: TE12 in W2, TE8 in W4

  • Pat Freiermuth: TE6 in W1

  • Brenton Strange: TE5 in W4

Freiermuth and Strange benefitted from a (maddening) trend against Cincinnati’s defense. Anyway, the larger point is that usage and on-field deployment should be our focus. A player’s ADP is just one data point. Hanging onto players because of their draft cost is a passive approach to our game. There are short-term pivots we can pick up even as we head into Week 5.

  • Tyler Higbee: 77.9% (Route Rate), 19.3% (TPRR), 22.5% (Slot Snap Rate)

  • Michael Mayer: 79.1%, 19.1%, 17.7%

  • Pat Freiermuth: 71.6%, 15.5%, 46.9%

Tyler Higbee is winning the war of attrition at TE for the Rams at eight targets per game over his last two. The Raiders got their TE1 back, but without a primary WR, Mayer becomes the main tight end as Bowers takes the alpha “WR” role.

Don’t let a decision in August negatively affect your squad come December. By following opportunity trends, we can lower our risk of another dud at such a volume-based position.

You (Don’t) Have to Have A Specific Draft Slot

Believe me when I say that I understand the emotional response to seeing your draft slot. There’s just something about where you sit in the order. As if, when you make your first pick relative to your leaguemates determines your rank before opening kickoff. That feels especially true when the guys at the front of the line have access to the real heavy hitters.

Gibbs and Bijan are really 1A & 1B omg pic.twitter.com/X7giDQakJl

— 𝔗𝔥𝔢 𝔇𝔢𝔱𝔯𝔬𝔦𝔱 𝔗𝔦𝔪𝔢𝔰 📰 (@the_det_times) October 6, 2026

Based on 12-team Yahoo ADP, the first five selections account for five All-Pro nominations and a hoard of Pro Bowl trips. Just having one of them is like a badge of honor. All anyone has to do is look at your RB1 or WR1 spot, check the name and give you the nod of approval.

But everyone needs more than one starter. And if Week 4 was any indication, production and draft price don’t have a direct correlation. Simply put, you can win from anywhere in the order. 

I took Hayden Winks' idea and built a fantasy points-over-replacement board using half-PPR scoring. Player ADP was the only rule, so I’d assume roster construction preferences would shake things up a bit. But there are landmines everywhere.

From the gamers who got the early picks to folks sitting at the 1.12, nobody was immune to disappointment. You can look at Team 9 with a bit of optimism, but RB2s have been hard to come by. And we’ve already talked about the ups and downs of drafting TEs. 

In either case, there’s another area where we can change our future. Back in August, I highlighted how I’m approaching the QB position. Using the points-over-replacement board from earlier, let’s zoom in on the first six rounds. A couple of guys stick out, but let’s focus on Jalen Hurts.

Here is every 3rd down passing attempt by Jalen Hurts in Week 3 vs. Bears pic.twitter.com/2ojOe64B2l

— Marcus Mosher (@Marcus_Mosher) September 29, 2026

Hurts was one of the examples I used as a viable early-round QB. I even emphasized his lack of passing efficiency, but his ability to create as a runner kept him in the conversation. But even that’s taken a step back.

  • Passing Success Rate: 37.3%, 24th (of 28 qualifiers – min. 80 dropbacks)

  • EPA per Dropback: -0.08, 21st 

  • QB Rushing Rate: 13.9%, 6th 

Similar to our expensive TEs, clutching our underperforming high-priced passers hoping for a turnaround puts us behind. Let’s see if we can apply a comparable process for identifying substitute QBs.

  • (Average) Passing Success Rate: 50.0%

  • Pass Rate Over Expectation: -0.1%

  • Rushing Rate: 12.0%

I pulled the average efficiency, team tendency and rushing numbers for the six hits within the top 12 QBs. Afterward, I lowered the values across the board to build an archetype of a passer you could find on your waiver wire that could give you passable results. Once again, the output points us in the right direction.

  • Bryce Young: Three top-8 finishes 

  • Tyler Shough: Three top-8 finishes 

  • Kirk Cousins: Three top-10 finishes

The other point to consider here is that the QBs themselves aren’t always to blame. Let’s revisit Hurts’ situation. No Dallas Goedert, DeVonta Smith was out this past week and the injuries continue to pile up along the offensive line. Lamar Jackson’s injury is another hurdle gamers will be managing for the next few weeks.

I took the next three games into consideration and found three potential passers who could get me to November.

  • Sam Darnold (Week 5-7 Opponents): 49ers, Broncos, Chiefs

  • Deshaun Watson: Jets, Ravens, Titans 

  • Jacoby Brissett: Lions, Rams, Broncos

Finding other options is something we do at RB and WR every Tuesday. In short, churning the QB position is no different and gives us flexibility that our draft spot couldn’t afford.

item.title: Moves to Make Before Week 5 Fantasy Football: Buy George Pickens, sell Quinshon Judkins
item.description: Alfredo Brown looks at players to buy and sell going into Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
Bye weeks are starting, injuries are piling up, and at this point you’ve either deleted the fantasy app from your phone, or you're looking to make some moves to stay competitive. After four weeks of action, some big names can be had for cheap, while it might be time to cash in on some outlier performances from certain players.

▶ PLAYERS TO BUY

George Pickens, WR, DAL

It’s been a rough start to the season for George Pickens and his fantasy managers. Pickens’ 20 percent target share in 2026 is nearly identical to his 21 percent target share in 2025. In fact, nearly everything is statistically the same except for his touchdown numbers. For the most part, Pickens has just been unlucky. Defensive pass interference calls and touchdown variance have kept his production down in an offense that leads the NFL in points per drive. The Cowboys should continue to pass the ball plenty, and CeeDee Lamb is unlikely to have 21 targets every week. Expect some positive regression for Pickens in the coming weeks.

Chase Brown, RB, CIN

Usage matters when it comes to running backs, and Chase Brown is getting plenty of it. He’s currently top 10 in snap share, opportunity share, routes run, route participation, and designed running back targets – all good signs. Unfortunately, the matchups have been tough for Brown to start the season. Three of Brown’s first four opponents rank in the bottom-eight in fantasy points allowed to running backs. This week he gets the Miami Dolphins, who have allowed the second-most fantasy points to running backs this season. With both Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins dealing with injuries this week, we could see Brown become the most important part of the Bengals’ offense, and his buy-low window could slam shut.

D’Andre Swift, RB, CHI

I like to bet on players getting volume in good offenses. It’s such a simple concept and tends to work out for fantasy football. The Bears appear to be a good offense regardless of the quarterback, and D’Andre Swift is the RB1 for Chicago, but the buy-low window may have opened for a brief moment. In Week 4, we got a classic Ben Johnson “time to teach you a lesson” moment when D’Andre Swift had a fumble in the second half, and the remaining three drives were given to Kyle Monangai, who finished with 30 carries in a lopsided win over the Jets. I wouldn’t read too much into that. The game was already out of reach, and the Bears just needed to run out the clock. Before Week 4, Swift was handling 64 percent of the backfield snaps, and nothing would indicate that we’re going to see a change going forward. If anything, we may see less Monangai as he deals with a finger injury. It’s also important to note that the Bears running backs have the second-easiest remaining strength of schedule and a playoff schedule that lends itself to three potential shootouts against the Bills, Packers, and Lions.

Carnell Tate, WR, TEN

Brace yourself, a top-five draft pick is being used like a top-five draft pick. The massive breakout game that fantasy managers have been waiting for finally happened. Tate just had nine receptions on 12 targets, for 145 yards and a touchdown. So why is this the time to buy? You’re certainly not buying low. This is more of a psychological thing. Tate’s fantasy managers have been frustrated for three weeks and likely didn’t have Tate in their lineup in Week 4 for the big breakout. If anything, they’ll likely be excited to sell high on Tate. The vibes around the Titans and Cam Ward are kinda gross, but if you look specifically at Tate, he’s totaled 21 targets over the last two weeks while having the seventh-highest first-read target rate in the NFL. The offense runs through Tate. Now going forward, the Titans’ wide receivers have the second-easiest remaining strength of schedule. This is a buy-high scenario that I’ll endorse because I believe we’ve just scratched the surface.

Carnell Tate since Week 2:

• 53% of the Titans’ total Air Yards@CDCarter13 thinks his production is here to stay : pic.twitter.com/t80mDh3Uio

— Rotoworld Football (@rotoworld_fb) October 5, 2026

Josh Downs, WR, IND

Week 4 was likely a fluke for Josh Downs, and it opened a buy-low window. He had a 14 percent target share, his lowest of the season, despite running the most routes of any Colts receiver. This isn’t a typical performance for Downs, who has been over a 29 percent target share in both games without Alec Pierce. Context around this previous game matters a lot in this instance. The Colts had an early lead and didn’t have to pass much in the second half. Daniel Jones only attempted 12 passes in the second half compared to 22 in the first. Downs did most of his work in the first half, seeing three of his four targets before halftime. This was more of an outlier with a game script issue, not a Josh Downs issue.

Jordan Mason, RB, MIN

A bit of looking ahead here with Mason on IR with a thumb injury and eligible to return in Week 7. We’ve learned that when Kyler Murray is given the opportunity to make a pass anywhere on the field, he’ll look to his running back early and often. Right now, Aaron Jones is reaping the benefits of the Murray checkdown offense, but eventually we’ll be back to a split backfield with Mason taking a large portion of the work. The thing is, Jones is nearly 32 years old, has missed significant time over the past three seasons, and has already dealt with an injury this year. If Jones were to miss time, Mason would instantly become a top 24 fantasy running back with a solid receiving floor and touchdown upside. The Vikings running backs have the fourth-easiest remaining strength of schedule and a bye week coming up in Week 6, making Mason an ideal buy-low candidate that has contingent upside and should be easy to acquire.

2026 NFL Week 5 Injury Report: Trouble in Cincy, LJax injury, updates on Kyle Monangai, Ladd McConkey
Track the injuries to know around the NFL, all in one place.
  • Mark Garcia,
  • Nic Bodiford,

▶ PLAYERS TO SELL

Quinshon Judkins, RB, CLE

I know the Browns have been winning games, but it hasn't exactly been because of Judkins. Through four weeks, Judkins is averaging just three yards per carry and has just one finish as a top 24 fantasy running back. To get that finish, he needed to have the second-best fantasy performance of his career and the highest receiving numbers of his career. Judkins has just one top-24 finish in his last seven games. While I think he might be a better player than what we’ve seen thus far, Judkins has proven to be a low-upside, touchdown-dependent player on a mediocre offense who does not typically catch passes. I know that might sound harsh, but we have film and data that say you should take this opportunity to sell high. The matchup against the Jets could give you one more week to sell high on Judkins, but I’d rather not risk needing him to fall into the end zone or have career-highs in receptions to maintain fantasy value.

Jameson Williams, WR, DET

We got the Jameson Williams game! All it took was for both of the Panthers’ starting cornerbacks to be out and a pass-heavy game script. Williams has been the poster child for inconsistent fantasy value. Would you believe me if I told you that over the last two seasons Williams has been outside the top 50 fantasy wide receivers nearly the same number of times he’s been in the top 20? I like the player as a talent, but if Sam LaPorta and Amon-Ra St. Brown are both playing, Williams is the third or fourth target on the team. He’s a boom/bust roller coaster. Your sell-high window may continue into next week against the Cardinals, who are without their top outside corner, Will Johnson, but the Lions have a bye in Week 6 and a less-than-favorable schedule for fantasy receivers going forward.

▶ PLAYERS TO STASH

If for any reason these guys are still on your waiver wire, you should stash them on your bench.

Emmett Johnson, RB, KC and Mike Washington Jr., RB, LV

These two rookies could be two of the best handcuff stashes in all of fantasy football. Johnson is the direct handcuff to one of the best running backs in all of fantasy, and Washington continues to make big plays for the Raiders in his limited reps. However, both of these guys are only rostered in 39 percent of Sleeper App leagues. If you have the space on your bench, I’d suggest stashing one or both of these rookie running backs, especially with Johnson and the Chiefs on a bye in Week 5.

Antonio Williams, WR, WAS

There’s an alternate universe where Antonio Williams finished Week 4 as a top 12 fantasy wide receiver. Williams had an 84-yard touchdown reception called back due to an illegal shift before the play even started. That’s a play that your leaguemates won't see in the stat line, but the coaches in Washington definitely noticed. Williams has watched his role grow, especially last week with Terry McLaurin out against the Colts. Both McLaurin and Stefon Diggs are 31 years or older. There’s a decent chance that one or both of them miss time at some point this season. Williams is a talented rookie with inside-outside versatility that should continue to see targets as the season goes on, specifically down the stretch from Week 12 on, where the Commanders receivers have the easiest strength of schedule leading up to and in the fantasy playoffs. You’ll likely see Williams get dropped as soon as McLaurin is back in the lineup as early as this week; if not, the Commanders have a bye in Week 7, where Williams will likely be dropped by a lot of fantasy managers.

Antonio Williams had a better day than the box score shows.

His 87-yd negated TD was elite. There haven't been that many guys in B&G with the strength (Garcon) and speed (Moss) who could score on that play over the years. Got 41 snaps and ran 30 routes without Terry playing.

— Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) October 5, 2026

Chris Bell, WR, MIA

Another talented rookie had a big touchdown reception called back for a silly reason. Malik Willis scrambled out of the pocket looking downfield, and as Bell worked his way back towards Willis, he had a toe on the boundary line, rendering him ineligible downfield. We haven’t had the monster breakout game just yet, but the signs are there. In Week 3, Bell had four receptions on eight targets, while in Week 4 Bell saw an 82 percent snap share, the highest of his career. If that touchdown had counted, he’d likely be all over the waiver wire lists for Week 5, but the stats don’t show “almost” touchdowns. Bell is probably available on your waiver wire now, and even if he isn’t, the Dolphins have a bye in Week 6, so you’re likely to see him get dropped.

item.title: 3 quarter season takeaways for the 49ers: How the Niners are putting it all together so far
item.description: The 49ers have been great on both sides of the ball. Here’s why.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are just about a quarter of the way into the season, and they’re undefeated so far, starting off 4-0 with wins over the Los Angeles Rams, Miami Dolphins, Arizona Cardinals, and Denver Broncos.

Through four games, the 49ers have been exceptional offensively, ranking first by a wide margin in EPA/play, while coming together strongly defensively, all while dealing with a large number of injuries.

Still, they’ve beaten two contenders, while establishing themselves as a real threat in the NFL behind MVP-level play from Brock Purdy.

So, through four weeks, let’s look at five quarter-season takeaways for the 49ers.

Brock Purdy excelling in several key categories

The Brock Purdy train has taken off, as the quarterback is currently the odds-on favorite to win MVP, being No. 1 on NFL.com’s MVP Ladder through four weeks.

He’s played extremely well thus far, including in a performance against the Denver Broncos where he still played quite well despite it being his “worst” game of the season. Purdy kept the ball out of harm’s way, took what the defense gave him, and still threw for 218 yards, two touchdowns, and no interceptions.

Through four weeks, Purdy is the clear leader in EPA per play and success rate at quarterback. He’s No. 1 in QBR. And he is also leveling up in key moments. Breaking it down by quarter, Purdy is the NFL’s top quarterback in EPA per play in both the third and fourth quarter, while ranking third in the NFL in the first quarter.

Purdy is also pushing the ball downfield, ranking first in yards per attempt, while completing nearly 70 percent of his passes and ranking fourth in completion rate over expected.

One category really caught my eye, though: Purdy’s excellence against the blitz.

Thus far, when blitzed, Purdy has completed 27 of 35 passes for 427 yards and seven touchdowns when blitzed, while not being sacked once on 11 pressures. He’s been the NFL’s best quarterback against the blitz and has seen the field very well, not making any turnover-worthy plays, which have been the issue in years past.

In 2025, Purdy’s completion rate dropped to 62.6 percent, and he had six of his 13 interceptions when blitzed, despite being blitzed on just 26.6 percent of his dropbacks. This year, he’s being blitzed at a 31.5 percent rate, and playing even better.

The story is simple: Purdy is making the plays while not taking any negative plays, regardless of situation.

The 49ers run game has a foundation

The Niners’ run game was an issue in 2025. They ranked 29th in EPA per rush and 24th in rushing success rate, as the explosives just weren’t there on the ground.

This season, the 49ers are 10th in EPA per rush and eighth in rushing success rate. Thus far, the 49ers are averaging 4.8 yards per carry, seventh in the league, while getting to 137.3 rushing yards per game, a top-six mark in the NFL.

That’s happened while Christian McCaffrey has averaged just 4.4 yards per carry and Kaelon Black has averaged 3.9 yards per carry, thanks to the wrinkles in the run game with Deebo Samuel and Brock Purdy’s ability to extend plays with his legs.

More importantly, the 49ers run game seems to have built a foundation again.

San Francisco’s offensive line has done a really good job over four weeks of keeping Brock Purdy up and limiting the pressure from opposing defenses. But they’ve also paved the way in the run game. San Francisco ranks fifth in yards before contact per rush (1.93 yards), and they’re also not getting negative plays in the run game, which was an issue last year.

Instead, the 49ers also rank sixth in percentage of runs with zero or negative yards before contact at 37.2 percent. So, they’re avoiding negative plays and averaging nearly five yards per tote.

The explosives still need to come. Christian McCaffrey and Kaelon Black also rank 24th and 45th, respectively, in yards after contact. But the 49ers are doing better on the ground and have a foundation there this year.

Limiting explosive plays

The 49ers have been the best team in the NFL at limiting explosive plays this season. In fact, their 3.5 percent explosive play rate allowed is the best of any team through four games since 2000. And that’s with a banged-up defensive line.

Raheem Morris has been exactly what the 49ers needed, and I’m slowly starting to compare him to DeMeco Ryans back during that monster 2022 defensive campaign. The 49ers are the No. 5 team defensively in DVOA, which, matched with the No. 1 rank on offense, has created a clear-cut contender.

Now, the 49ers are 26th in pressure rate, but part of that is attributed to teams looking to get the ball out quickly. Subsequently, they’re sixth in ESPN’s pass rush win rate, and it helps to limit explosive plays when linebackers Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw fly to the ball.

I’ve been impressed with how Morris has created pressure with his personnel up front on the defensive line, but also with how the 49ers have played coverage through four weeks. After struggling last season at times, the 49ers secondary has looked the part in a big way so far.

That includes growth from safeties Marques Sigle and Malik Mustapha, as well as from Renardo Green and the newcomer Jack Jones, who have all played roles in the secondary so far.

Overall, you’re starting to see a defense gel in a new scheme, and this unit should only get better with healthy players. It’s been a very promising start to the 49ers season.

item.title: Giants signing QB Jake Haener to 53-man roster
item.description: The Giants will have three quarterbacks on their 53-man roster.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants will have three quarterbacks on their 53-man roster.

Per Mike Garafolo of NFL Network, New York is signing Jake Haener back to the active roster from the team's practice squad.

Haener had previously been promoted to the 53-man roster after Jaxson Dart suffered his season-ending knee injury. But Haener was waived and re-signed to the practice squad after the club traded for J.J. McCarthy.

With three QBs on the active roster, the Giants will be able to designate either McCarthy or Haener as the emergency third quarterback.

At 3-1, the Giants will be on the road to face the Commanders in Week 5.

item.title: Chargers sign OL Daniel Brunskill to practice squad
item.description: The Chargers are adding veteran OL Daniel Brunskill to the practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
The Chargers are adding another offensive lineman who has familiarity with offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel.

On Tuesday, the Chargers announced the signing of former 49ers and Dolphins offensive tackle Daniel Brunskill to their practice squad. In a corresponding move, the Chargers are also releasing defensive tackle Jordan Jefferson.

Along with the signing, the Chargers are also activating the 21-day practice windows for fullback Scott Matlock and offensive lineman Branson Taylor. Both players have been on IR since the preseason.

Brunskill spent the first two seasons of his career with the Atlanta Falcons on their practice squad. In the spring of 2019, he also played one season in the now-defunct Alliance of American Football for the San Diego Fleet.

From 2019 to 2022, Brunskill was a member of the San Francisco 49ers where he overlapped with McDaniel. He started 42 of 61 games for the Niners during that span, including 33 starts of a possible 34 during the 2020 and 2021 regular seasons. From 2023-2024, Brunskill started 24 of 31 games for the Titans.

The 32-year old Brunskill was most recently with the Dolphins in 2025 where he started five games for McDaniel while playing in 16 total contests.

item.title: Jerry Jones says Cowboys’ ‘door is open’ before trade deadline, and there’s reason to believe him
item.description: With the NFC East ripe for the Cowboys to take it, this could be Jones' best shot to contend in years.
item.content:encoded:
Rewind back roughly 18 months and the Dallas Cowboys’ building strategy was straightforward.

Draft and develop homegrown talent. Extend the success stories like quarterback Dak Prescott, wide receiver CeeDee Lamb and cornerback DaRon Bland. Draft and develop more to offset the cost of such contract extensions. Cost-effective holes might be bandaged via free agency and trade, but little else.

As of early 2025, Cowboys team owner and general manager Jerry Jones’ talk was mostly just that: talk. His “all-in” assertion drew scrutiny for how little it seemed to align with his actions. He wasn’t living up to the risk-taking reputation he’d developed in the 1990s during the Cowboys’ Super Bowl run. He wasn’t seeking and striking gold the way he’d done in the oil business in which he made some of his money. The Cowboys were surprisingly methodical, if slow and late on extensions relative to their counterparts.

A Cowboys team chock full of talent but repeatedly underachieving seemed passive in chasing those final upgrades.

Back then, comments like Jones made Wednesday morning would have sounded hollow.

“The door is always open to get better,” he said during an appearance on Dallas radio station 105.3 The Fan. “I know that’s almost a cliché. I’m never shut down from trying to get something that would really advance the needle. Especially one that could do it now and into the future. 

“Again, I said at the start of training camp: I’m willing to put some things out there that lean more today than they would be three years from now.”

Jones’ actions since May 2025 give reason to believe him.

It was then that the Cowboys dealt a third-round pick (and swapped a fifth and six) to the Pittsburgh Steelers to acquire talented but volatile receiver George Pickens.

By late August 2025, one week before the Cowboys’ season opener, Jones had dealt three-time first-team All-Pro edge rusher Micah Parsons to the Green Bay Packers rather than extend Parsons. The Packers sent the Cowboys defensive tackle Kenny Clark and first-round picks in 2026 and 2027 as compensation.

At the trade deadline last year, Jones made arguably as stunning a trade: In the most dramatic move since their 2018 trade-deadline deal for wide receiver Amari Cooper, the Cowboys were sending a 2027 first-round pick, plus a 2026 second and defensive tackle Mazi Smith, to the New York Jets for defensive tackle Quinnen Williams.

The Cowboys would later trade up to select safety Caleb Downs in the first round of the 2026 NFL Draft. In August, they’d trade a third and sixth to the Steelers for offensive tackle Broderick Jones and a fourth. 

And last week, after the Steelers and cornerback Joey Porter Jr.’s negotiation stalemate reached a point of no return, Dallas acted to improve its defense. The Cowboys sent a 2028 second-round pick and 2027 sixth to acquire Porter. Porter played 25 defensive snaps (45%) in the Cowboys’ 34-30 win at the Houston Texans.

Will the Cowboys chase still another piece before the Nov. 10 trade deadline? At 2-2, with a Tampa Bay Buccaneers team led by a backup quarterback visiting on Thursday, there’s reason to believe the Cowboys will seriously explore an addition.

Dallas’ schedule is highly manageable between now and the Nov. 10 trade deadline, with .500 and below teams in the Bucs, Green Bay Packers, Philadelphia Eagles, Arizona Cardinals and Indianapolis Colts. The division is wide open, especially as quarterback injuries slow the New York Giants and Washington Commanders, while an Eagles team adjusting to a new offensive scheme reckons with the abrupt retirement of six-time Pro Bowl right tackle Lane Johnson.

The Cowboys offense is potent while its defense improves. And Jones knows that a deep list of his starters is up for contracts in the spring, so this core may be his best chance to contend in the next few years.

“We’ve got a trade deadline coming up where you can do some things,” Jones said. “Let’s see what happens. You obviously see that we’re in a transition to some degree in the club, but the transition is so that we can win now as opposed to the transition addressing totally two to three years for now. …

“I’m open. We’re open.”

item.title: NFL Survivor contest picks, predictions, advice, strategy: My favorite Week 5 selections
item.description: Matt Russell runs through his Week 5 NFL Survivor pool plays, giving his favorite picks to help you advance.
item.content:encoded:
The appeal of NFL Survivor contests is that even though nothing of significance happened on the field in Week 4, there's still plenty of intrigue.

Another fork in the road was created with a choice between two double-digit favorites — Baltimore and Minnesota. The Ravens survived for their contestants without Lamar Jackson in the second half, while the Vikings' offense again opted out of scoring touchdowns but beat the Dolphins 15-10. 

The Bills' loss to the Patriots was the only plausible pothole for last week, as evidenced by the distribution numbers from Circa Sports' massive Survivor contest:

Here is my Week 5 survivor pool analysis.

The number of remaining participants in your pool also changes the calculus when it comes to strategy. After all, the fewer the entrants, the less conceptual risk is necessary each week. 

Each week (until we've exhausted all reasonable paths of survival), we look at the Survivor Contest landscape, and the best options available, while understanding that it matters who you've already taken, and what you might be giving up by burning a team that week.

Week 5 moneylines

How likely is a team to win and you'll advance? The betting market provides the answer to that each week with the moneyline, which we can convert to an implied win probability.

Market power ratings

It's not as simple as picking the team most likely to win, because once you use that team, you can't use it again. What is simple is that if you're going to make it through the 18-week season, then you need to use 18 teams. That means, at some point, you'll be trusting the 18th-best team in the NFL — an unnerving thought. 

Here's a list of the current top 18 teams (with help from the betting market), and an estimation of their value to the point spread: 

  • Rams: 19.2

  • Seahawks, Jaguars: 18.1

  • Bills: 17.6

  • Chiefs, 49ers: 17.3

  • Bengals: 16.7

  • Texans, Broncos: 16.2

  • Cowboys: 15.7

  • Bears, Lions, Patriots: 14.9

  • Vikings: 14

  • Steelers: 13.5

  • Colts: 13

  • Raiders, Falcons: 12.7

Picking the most likely team to win each week, or the highest available team on this list above, means that you're giving up the opportunity to use it later, and while every week is technically created equal, trusting a team in September is nerve-wracking, but doing so at some point in December is real tension. 

Week 5's top choices

As we look at the best options for Week 5 and onward, we'll be factoring in the decision tree that will sprout from that pick. The implied probability derived from the moneyline should answer any questions about why the favorite should win, but the nuance is found in what you're giving up by using it now and not later (with a projected point spread projection for those matchups). 

Cowboys (79.4%) over Buccaneers 

Week 5 looks to be pretty complicated, especially if you don't get around to making a pick until the weekend. 

The only favorite of -200 or shorter (66.6% win probability or higher) to play at home this week does so on Thursday Night Football, with the Cowboys hosting the Buccaneers. 

Tampa Bay (+2.5) lost 17-14 at home against the Packers, with Jalon Daniels at the helm, so there should be less mystery about what the Bucs offense is capable of on a short week. Even against the Cowboys' not-remotely-big 'D'.  

We almost always know what we'll get with the Cowboys' offense, though. Especially at home.

Estimated Availability: 99.6%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 8 vs. Cardinals (DAL -9.5)

  • Week 11 vs. Titans (DAL -10)

  • Week 17 vs. Giants (DAL -7)

In a regular, 18-week Survivor format, you don't need to save the Cowboys for possible use on Thanksgiving (like you might in Circa's). While fading the Cardinals, Titans, or late-season Giants (who may be letting J.J. McCarthy take the offense for a test drive) is appealing, there might be better alternatives in those weeks than there are in this one, relatively speaking. 

For example: 

  • Week 8: Bengals over Titans

  • Week 11: Chiefs over Cardinals, Bills over Dolphins

  • Week 17: Jaguars over Commanders, Falcons over Saints, Bills over Dolphins

Texans (76.3%) over Titans 

Which of the many road favorites can we trust? 

Sure, the one that's 0-4. Naturally.

The Texans' losses to the Bills, Bengals, Colts and Cowboys all came against teams that are much better than Tennessee, which just lost to one-half of the Ravens offense last week, and have surpassed a calendar year since they beat a team quarterbacked by someone other than Shedeur Sanders or Chris Oladokun (and much longer than that at home).

For all the trepidation surrounding the disappointing start to the season for Houston, the Texans haven't lost to a team remotely resembling the Titans.

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 7 vs. Giants (HOU -7)

  • Week 18 vs. Titans (HOU -10.5)

Another reason to use the Cowboys on Thursday is that you can save the Texans for two weeks from now (at home against the Giants), ideally, at a time when they've already tasted victory once this season. Plus, in Week 7, the best options are the Panthers at home to the Bucs and the Jets hosting the Dolphins, as the Titans host the Browns — a rare scenario where Tennessee has a reasonable chance to win. 

Jaguars (75.9%) over Eagles 

To get to the next home favorite, you'd have to go down to the Patriots at home to the Raiders — a matchup that looked far more inviting before the season than it does now. 

The Jaguars don't reside in England (in the wild or in the form of an NFL franchise), but they do regularly make a two-week trip overseas — a home away from home, if you will. Through four weeks, the case could be made that Jacksonville has been the most consistently impressive team this season, and the Eagles seem to be falling apart at the seams, with holes in the offensive line, and injuries to Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith, and Dallas Goedert. 

Estimated Availability: 49.4%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 10 at Titans (JAX -9.5)

  • Week 12 vs. Titans (JAX -12.5)

  • Week 14 vs. Steelers (JAX -6)

  • Week 17 vs. Commanders (JAX -7.5)

If you think the Eagles can muster enough to topple Jacksonville in London, or just rather try to get the "Survivor week" over early with Dallas, the Jags have two meetings with the Titans shortly after getting back to the mainland and their post-European excursion bye week. Not to mention the late-season game with the Commanders referenced as an option above as part of our argument to take the Cowboys this week. 

You can find more valuable betting analysis from Yahoo Sports betting contributor, Matt Russell, at THE WINDOW.

item.title: Is Kellen Moore’s seat hot after loss to the Falcons?
item.description: Moore said New Orleans was unprepared for Monday night’s loss to Atlanta.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints’ 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night felt different.

It was completely embarrassing.

It was not just another loss. It was a total failure across all three phases on a night that was so special to the city and the fanbase.

The Saints had an opportunity to make a statement in front of a nationally televised audience, and they blew it.

And now, it’s fair to ask how hot Kellen Moore’s seat is after a 1-3 start.

Moore did not hide from the performance afterward. He repeatedly acknowledged that the Saints were not prepared for Monday night’s game, which is frustrating to hear after knowing how important this game was and how much it meant to the organization.

It would be easier to accept if it were an isolated occurrence.

But it hasn’t been.

The Saints under Kellen Moore have now trailed by double digits 16 times since the start of the 2025 season, the most in the NFL over that span. Monday night was another example, as Atlanta jumped out to a 14-0 lead in the first quarter and extended it to 24-7 by halftime.

The problem isn’t simply that New Orleans has fallen behind. It’s that Moore has been asked repeatedly why his team continues to struggle to open games, and his answers have consistently come back to some version of needing to look at things, make adjustments and figure out what went wrong.

At some point, those answers have to turn into results.

The Saints scored just six total first-quarter points through their first four games and have been forced to play from behind in every game this season. Under Moore, New Orleans has failed to score in the first quarter 14 times. That puts immense pressure on Moore to fix the preparation and execution issues that have followed his team into another season.

There is still plenty of football left to play, and firing a head coach after four games would be an extreme move. But this is also Year 2 for Moore, so there’s no excuse of this being his first rodeo. The Saints expected progress after a six-win first season, and instead they are 1-3 after getting embarrassed by their biggest rival on Monday night.

Moore has repeatedly said the Saints need to look at themselves.

Now, the question is how long the organization will continue waiting for the answers to translate onto the field before they take a look at him.

item.title: Colts sign veteran pass rusher Carl Lawson to practice squad
item.description: The Colts added veteran defensive end Carl Lawson as injuries continue to thin out their pass-rush rotation.
item.content:encoded:
The Colts added some veteran help to their defensive front Wednesday, signing defensive end Carl Lawson to the practice squad.

Indianapolis also released tight end Kenny Fletcher Jr. from the practice squad to make room for Lawson, who had previously worked out for the Colts on Sept. 23.

The timing is pretty easy to understand. Arden Key is expected to miss time with an injury, while Micheal Clemons is already on injured reserve, leaving the Colts thinner than they would like at defensive end. Lawson gives them an experienced option who already has familiarity with defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo’s system.

Lawson played under Anarumo in Cincinnati during the 2019 and 2020 seasons, and 2020 was arguably the best year of his career. He recorded 64 pressures that season and continued to establish himself as a disruptive rotational pass rusher. That familiarity should help if Indianapolis eventually needs to elevate him to the active roster.

The 31-year-old has played eight NFL seasons with the Bengals, Jets, Cowboys and Ravens, appearing in 90 games with 34 starts. Over that span, he has recorded 32 sacks, 122 quarterback hits, 32 tackles for loss and four forced fumbles. His role has decreased in recent years, though, and he played just 26 defensive snaps for Baltimore last season.

This should not be viewed as some major solution to the Colts’ pass-rush problems. Lawson is being added to the practice squad in October for a reason, and expecting him to suddenly become the player he was several years ago would be unrealistic.

Still, the move makes sense considering the state of the defensive line.

Indianapolis enters its Week 5 matchup against Pittsburgh ranked 31st in total defense, allowing 423.8 yards per game. The Colts have struggled to consistently affect opposing quarterbacks, and injuries have now taken away two veterans from an edge group that was already short on proven difference-makers.

Lawson at least gives Anarumo another player he knows and trusts, along with someone who has shown in the past that he can create pressure when used in the right role. If Key remains out for multiple games, it would not be surprising to see Lawson elevated and given rotational snaps sooner rather than later.

For now, he gives the Colts some needed insurance at a position that has quickly become even thinner.

item.title: Odell Beckham Jr. signs with the Vikings practice squad
item.description: Former NY Giants star receiver Odell Beckham Jr. looks to extend his career with the Minnesota Vikings
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Vikings announced Thursday morning that they’ve signed former New York Giants star wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. to their practice squad.

The Giants originally signed Beckham to their 90-man roster back on June 1, and while the ball didn’t find Beckham in games, he looked solid in practice and preseason. He ultimately made the Giants’ initial 53-man roster after final cutdowns.

However, he only saw 20 snaps over the first three games with the Giants before being released prior to Week 4. Beckham remained a fan favorite in New York, receiving ovations every time he got on the field, but his second stint as a Giant ended with no catches.

It was reported that Beckham had no interest in signing with the Giants’ practice squad and wanted to go somewhere where he had a better chance to play. The Vikings are looking for a spark on offense, and head coach Kevin O’Connell is familiar with Beckham from their time together with the Los Angeles Rams.

item.title: Vic Fangio says it’s possible the Eagles are playing Jalen Carter too much
item.description: The Eagles DC talks late-game collapse, pass rush concerns, and depth issues.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles are having a rough week, and as they prepare for the Jaguars in London, defensive coordinator Vic Fangio spoke to reporters about their late-game struggles against the Rams, what he thinks of the secondary, and about Jalen Carter’s work load with a cast.

As the injuries continue to stack up, Fangio was asked how he feels about the depth on defense:

“It’s being challenged right now, so we’ll see. But I think in certain places we’re good and others, you cross your fingers.”

When later asked about which positions lack depth, he coyly replied, “You’ll have to figure that out yourself.”

Here’s what else the DC had to say:

On the late game struggles

Fangio said that they struggled to make a play and he struggled to make the right call late in the game against the Rams, and with a veteran QB like Matthew Stafford, that’s a bad combination.

“We didn’t get it done. You know, we played great for 10 drives, but the last two, we didn’t.”

The DC clarified that the defense played 83 total snaps, including penalties, and while it might have a small affect on things, ultimately, they need to find a way to finish.

On the secondary

Fangio thought that Michael Carter did a good job on Sunday.

He was asked about Jonathan Jones having to come in after Quinyon Mitchell was sidelined, and the DC said he was happy with how the CB stepped up.

“I thought [Jonathan Jones] did good for really his first action in a long time. If you remember, he missed the tail end of training camp and hadn’t had any action since whenever, one of the early preseason games and though he’d come in there and did a good job. He does a good job preparing and he was ready to go.”

The DC said that they are hopeful that Quinyon Mitchell will be available this weekend, but said they’ll find out more as the week goes on.

He was also complimentary of new DB Kenny Moore and how he’s preparing to contribute.

“[Kenny Moore]‘s getting closer. He’s done a great job learning, [we’re] trying to get him to learn two positions to be part of nickel or dime, and safety. But he got in there for a play or two at the end.“

On the pass rush

“I thought it was inconsistent.”

The DC said that they haven’t been consistently really good in one-on-ones, and while they might be affected by chips, when they are getting one-on-ones, they’re not getting it done on a consistent basis.

Ultimately, though, Fangio said that he’s still confident that the pass rush will get to a level that he wants to see.

“I just believe in the guys. A lot of times too, we’ve lost two sacks the last two games due to penalties. Sometimes the ball’s coming out quick, like previous some games. I know you guys have a love affair with the sack stat, but the ball’s coming out quick a lot.”

On playing time for players

  • Fangio said that LB Jeremiah Trotter Jr. played very well against the Rams, and probably earned some more playing time as a result.
  • The DC was also asked about Jordan Davis only taking 35 percent of the defensive snaps, to which Fangio admitted that they probably need to get him on the field more. He explained that it was more of a result of personnel the Rams were in — they had been playing a lot of three tight ends in the weeks before the Eagles game, but then went with more three receiver looks on Sunday, which changed the game.
  • He admitted that Jalen Carter’s wrist injury affected him more on Sunday against the Rams than in previous games, and when asked if the DT is playing more than he should be, Fangio replied, “Possibly.”

On the Jaguars offense

“They’re really good on offense. The quarterback is athletic, got a big arm, he’s got a good group of receivers to throw it to. Their running back, 33 [RB Bhayshul Tuten] runs really good, kind of a new guy on the scene and they do a good job. They got a very varied running game, a lot of different types of runs, multiple run game and they’re good at it.”

Other notables

  • Fangio said that safety Andrew Mukuba has been playing well all season, and he’s real pleased with where he is in his development.
  • He noted that Jalyx Hunt just needs to continue doing the little things consistently.
  • The DC said LB Jihaad Campbell has been coming along, and is getting better each game against both the run and pass game.

item.title: Vikings Sign Odell Beckham Jr., Jeshaun Jones to Practice Squad
item.description: Well, didn’t see that coming
item.content:encoded:
With a couple of open spots on the practice squad, the Minnesota Vikings filled them on Wednesday with a pair of wide receivers, one of which you may have even heard of before.

Well, if you’re a Vikings fan, you’ve heard of both of them, but one of them. . .yeah, didn’t see this coming.

The Vikings have announced the signings of wide receivers Jeshaun Jones and Odell Beckham Jr. to the practice squad.

The Vikings brought Jones back after he served his three-game suspension for violating the league’s substance abuse policy and waiving him earlier in the week, but you don’t care about that at the moment, do you?

Beckham Jr. really needs no introduction. He was drafted by the New York Giants out of Louisiana State in the first round of the 2014 NFL Draft, after which he won the NFL’s Offensive Rookie of the Year Award and has twice been named a Second-Team NFL All-Pro (2015, 2016). In his career, he has 575 receptions for 7,987 receiving yards and 59 touchdowns.

His career has dropped off significantly since 2020, when he suffered a torn ACL midway through the season as a member of the Cleveland Browns. He returned to Cleveland for the 2021 season but had disagreements with the way he was being used in the Cleveland offense, leading to his release. He landed with the Los Angeles Rams and was a part of their Super Bowl championship team. He scored a touchdown in that Super Bowl, but he suffered another ACL injury during that game as well, one that caused him to miss the entire 2022 season.

In 2023, Beckham signed with the Baltimore Ravens and had 35 receptions for 565 yards and three scores. He was released by the Ravens ahead of free agency in 2024 and signed with Miami. He started the season on the Physically Unable to Perform List and wound up being released in December, appearing in nine games and making just nine catches. He did not play in 2025, and for part of the 2025 season served a six-game suspension for violating the league’s performance-enhancing drug policy.

Beckham attempted a comeback with the Giants this season and made the 53-man roster out of training camp, but was released after three games without recording a catch.

I’m not sure how high the expectations should be for OBJ at this point in his career or how much juice he has left in the proverbial tank. But he’s a member of the Vikings now, so what does everyone think about this development?

item.title: ESPN's 2027 Super Bowl telecast will stream on Disney+

item.content:encoded:
The Super Bowl is coming to Disney+.

The Walt Disney Co. announced Wednesday that ESPN’s telecast of the NFL’s marquee event on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., will be available to Disney+ subscribers. The company also said Disney+ will carry two ESPN “Monday Night Football” games in the current season.

ESPN is producing the Super Bowl for the first time in its history. The game is airing on Disney’s broadcast network ABC, which last carried the game in 2006, and on ESPN and the ESPN app.

The addition of Disney+ makes the game available to casual fans who may not have cable or subscribe to a sports TV channel. The Super Bowl is the most-watched TV event of the year, with audiences exceeding 120 million viewers in recent years.

Streaming platforms are bringing in additional advertising revenue for the networks that carry the game.

Read more:2026 Super Bowl scores 124.9 million viewers, second-largest audience in history

In 2025, the Fox telecast of Super Bowl LIX averaged 13.6 million viewers on Tubi, the ad-supported streaming service owned by the network’s parent company. Fox was able to sell streaming-only ads on the telecast at around $2 million for a 30-second commercial. The spots aired in the commercial breaks for local Fox TV affiliates.

Disney is offering advertisers the opportunity to buy streaming-only ads across Disney+, the ESPN app, Hulu Live and Fubo. The company has already sold out the commercial time on the ESPN and ABC telecasts with some 30-second spots going for $10 million.

As a lead-up to the game, Disney+ will carry ESPN’s “Monday Night Football” matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles on Oct. 26 and another contest later in the season.

Disney+ has been adding sports to its lineup, with select ESPN college football games and Formula E races now available on the platform.

item.title: Former Giants WR Odell Beckham Jr. being signed to Vikings' practice squad
item.description: Odell Beckham Jr. is reportedly signing to the Minnesota Vikings' practice squad after being released by the Giants on Sept. 29.
item.content:encoded:
Odell Beckham Jr. has found his next opportunity.

The former star wide receiver is signing to the Minnesota Vikings' practice squad, according to ESPN and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, after being released by the Giants on Sept. 29.

Beckham had just one target and zero catches over three games (just 20 snaps) with New York, resulting in Big Blue making the "tough" decision to let him go.

"Tough, but we just weren’t getting enough," John Harbaugh said last week. "It just wasn’t working for us. I told him I wanted to be able to get more. I wanted him to be able to do more. I wanted to get him on the field more.

"And we just, for whatever reason, we weren’t able to do it. Put it on us. We weren’t able to get it done. At this point in time, that’s kind of where we were. And needed to move on."

Harbaugh indicated that the decision was "nothing about Odell, nothing that he could do," adding that they needed "more out out of that [roster] spot."

Beckham will now reunite with Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell, who was the Los Angeles Rams offensive coordinator when the WR was with the team in 2021. 

Over two stints with the franchise, Beckham finished his Giants career with 390 catches for 5,476 yards and 44 touchdowns. Overall, the 33-year-old has made 575 receptions for 7,987 yards and 59 touchdowns across 122 games.

item.title: Odell Beckham Jr. taking J.J. McCarthy's number after joining Vikings
item.description: Odell Beckham Jr., the gifted but aging and oft-injured wide receiver, has joined the practice squad of the Vikings, who rank last in the NFL in passing.
item.content:encoded:
If it appeared as if Odell Beckham Jr. would bookend his NFL career playing in separate stints with the New York Giants, apparently not.

The once electrifying but aging and oft-injured wide receiver joined the Minnesota Vikings' practice squad on Wednesday, Oct. 7. The 11th-year veteran will wear No. 9 in Minnesota, ironically the jersey just vacated by former Vikes quarterback J.J. McCarthy, aka "Nine," whom the Giants obtained in a trade on Sept. 28.

Though Beckham hasn't caught even 40 passes in a season since 2021 − which he split between the Cleveland Browns and Los Angeles Rams, catching a touchdown in Super Bowl 56 and winning a ring with the latter (and tearing his ACL in the process) − he might prove to be an asset to the Vikings, who rank last in the league in passing offense. No wide receiver on the team has even 15 catches, though that's partially due to perennial Pro Bowler Justin Jefferson's ankle injury, which kept him out of Sunday's win over the Miami Dolphins. OBJ's ability to freelance, especially in three- and four-receiver sets, might also dovetail nicely with new Vikes quarterback Kyler Murray, who was famous for improvising on broken plays during his time in Arizona.

And though the Pro Bowl days of Beckham, a first-round pick of the Giants in 2014 − he eclipsed 1,300 receiving yards in each of his first three seasons but hasn't approached that figure since − are well behind him, so is his reputation for brashness and flamboyance. A quiet leader in the latter part of his career, he could also be a welcome figure alongside Jefferson, who also hails from LSU, in the Vikings locker room.

Minnesota, one of four remaining undefeated teams in the league, visits the New Orleans Saints on Sunday in what will be something of a homecoming for Beckham and Jefferson.

The Giants released OBJ, who will turn 34 next month, from their 53-man roster last week. He was targeted once but had zero receptions in three games and played a total of 20 snaps for New York in his brief second tour of duty with the organization.

Beckham recently lamented his recent time in New York on Instagram.

"(I don't know) why they even gave me the run along," Beckham wrote. "I coulda really been playing this year somewhere and making a impact."

Now he might get his chance. Still, OBJ's last regular-season reception came in 2024 as a member of the Miami Dolphins.

If Beckham ultimately plays the Vikings, they would become his sixth NFL team.

item.title: AFC North Week 4 recap: Browns take the lead
item.description: The Browns sit atop the AFC North after four weeks.
item.content:encoded:
An unfamiliar face sits atop the competitive AFC North after four weeks of the season. Here are the latest updates from around the division:

Cleveland Browns (3-1)

The Cleveland Browns won their third consecutive game with a 27-24 victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers, taking the lead in the division in the process due to tiebreakers.

Deshaun Watson’s resurgence on the field continued into Week 4 as he led the Browns’ offense to set up a career-long 56-yard field goal from Andre Szmyt to take the lead with 10 seconds remaining in regulation. Watson finished the game 24 of 33 for 268 yards, a touchdown, and an interception while also losing a fumble. The story of the game for Cleveland’s offense, however, was the play of their two rookie wide receivers. Second-rounder Denzel Boston led the team with 89 yards on four catches while first-rounder KC Concepcion was second with 64 yards on five catches. Harold Fannin Jr. caught Watson’s lone touchdown. Quinshon Judkins led the team in rushing, but found little success with just 53 yards on 17 carries. The second-year back did find his way into the end zone once, though.

The Browns’ defense made life difficult for Aaron Rodgers, sacking him five times while coming down with two interceptions against the future Hall-of-Fame quarterback. Denzel Ward snagged the first interception in the second quarter, while the second came from Grant Delpit on the final play of the game. Cleveland lost Mason Graham early in the game with what was later revealed to be a sprained MCL and ankle. The timeline for the 2025 fifth-overall pick is currently unknown.

Baltimore Ravens (3-1)

The Ravens improved to 3-1 with a 24-18 home win over the Tennessee Titans, but an ankle injury to Lamar Jackson overshadowed the victory.

Jackson was stellar in the first half, completing 15 of 20 passes for 222 yards and two touchdowns before an ankle injury on a sack sidelined him for the remainder of the game. The NFL world now awaits clarity on the status of Jackson’s injury and how much time, if any, he may miss. Tyler Huntley replaced Jackson for the second half as the offense came to a screeching halt. Zay Flowers was on his way to another dominant outing before Jackson exited the game, finishing the day with a team-high 118 receiving yards and a touchdown on eight catches. Mark Andrews caught Jackson’s other touchdown as he found the end zone for the first time this season. Derrick Henry struggled to find running room against his old team, racking up 73 yards and a touchdown on 23 carries for just 3.2 yards per carry. Alongside Jackson, Baltimore also lost Durham Smythe to a torn Achilles, Andrew Vorhees to a foot injury, and Marlon Humphrey to a calf injury during the game.

The Ravens’ defense has been under heavy scrutiny to start the season, and that was not helped by an up-and-down performance against a weak Titans’ offense. The game started strong with a Trenton Simpson interception on the first drive, but many of the same issues popped up throughout the game, including an inability to finish sacks and missed tackles. Undrafted rookie Ethan Burke recorded the team’s lone sack on Cam Ward. Kyle Hamilton forced a fumble on rookie first-rounder Carnell Tate, which was recovered by Malaki Starks. Starks also recovered an onside kick to ice the game.

Pittsburgh Steelers (2-2)

The Steelers dropped to 2-2 with a 27-24 loss on the road to the Browns.

Pittsburgh rallied from a 21-10 hole at halftime, falling three points short in the end. Rodgers completed 22 of 40 passes for 299 yards and three touchdowns with two interceptions, although the second came with just 10 seconds remaining in the game. DK Metcalf had by far his best game of the season with five catches for 115 yards. Roman Wilson, Darnell Washington, and Pat Freiermuth were the recipients of Rodgers’ three touchdowns. Jaylen Warren had another strong performance with 93 rushing yards on 17 carries to go with three catches for 33 yards.

The Steelers’ defense forced two turnovers on the night, a fumble forced and recovered by T.J. Watt, and an interception by Robert Spears-Jennings. Watt and Payton Wilson had the team’s two sacks on Watson. Pittsburgh lost Derrick Harmon during the game to a foot injury and Jamel Dean to an ankle injury. Harmon has since been placed on injured reserve, meaning he will miss at least four games. Dean is not expected to join Harmon on injured reserve.

Cincinnati Bengals (2-2)

After starting the season 2-0, the Bengals have now dropped back-to-back games following a 22-17 home loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Joe Burrow had a tough outing while losing his top two wide receivers during the game. Burrow finished 39 of 54 for 428 yards, a touchdown, and two picks. Tee Higgins had a team-high 157 receiving yards on 11 catches before a groin injury knocked him out of the game in the fourth quarter. Ja’Marr Chase left the game much earlier with a concussion, leaving Burrow possibly without his top two weapons next week against the Miami Dolphins. Cincinnati had next to nothing in the run game, with Chase Brown leading the team with just 10 yards on nine carries. The Bengals finished the game with only 23 total rushing yards.

Cincinnati’s defense sacked Trevor Lawrence four times, with Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe, Myles Murphy, and Kris Jenkins Jr. all getting a sack.

item.title: Houston Texans Defense: Serious Problem?
item.description: The Houston Texans entered the 2026 season with sky-high expectations after their dominant display the season prior. They are pretty much stacked at all three levels of the defense, but somehow, things have not looked the way they used to. Regression is always possible in the NFL, but the drop-off from one year to the […]
item.content:encoded:
The Houston Texans entered the 2026 season with sky-high expectations after their dominant display the season prior.

They are pretty much stacked at all three levels of the defense, but somehow, things have not looked the way they used to. Regression is always possible in the NFL, but the drop-off from one year to the next, especially without losing much talent, has been troublesome.

If you look back at the start of last season, the Texans’ defense also started somewhat slow and did not immediately become the dominant unit we eventually saw. The offense could not get much of anything going, and the defense was doing everything it could to keep Houston in games.

This year, it has been almost the complete opposite.

Houston’s offense has looked far better when fully healthy. The Texans have put up 30 points per game when their best wide receiver, Nico Collins, has been on the field. He missed two games this season, and the offense struggled tremendously without him, but that is a story for a different day.

The reality of the situation is that quarterback C.J. Stroud gave the Texans a late fourth-quarter lead in three of their first four games. In each of those situations, the defense had an opportunity to get a stop and close out the game, but they were unable to do so.

That is a major reason why this team is sitting at 0-4.

Defensively, the Texans have immense talent, and there is no questioning that. The issue is that it feels like the players are not always being put in the best situations to succeed, especially when it comes to the scheme in certain situations.

This is a defense loaded with players who have already proven they can play at an elite level. When a unit this talented continues to struggle in crucial moments, eventually you have to look beyond the players themselves and figure out what needs to change.

In order for Houston to have any chance of turning this season around, the defense simply has to be better. The good news is that there is plenty of reason to believe that will happen. There is far too much talent on this roster for this unit to continue playing at this level.

Defensive end Will Anderson Jr. is already having a Defensive Player of the Year-caliber season and has been practically unstoppable through the first four games. He has established himself as the anchor of this defense and continues to make an impact on a weekly basis.

The Texans now need the rest of the defense to follow his lead.

Starting 0-4 is obviously far from ideal, and Houston has put itself in a difficult position moving forward. However, this does not feel like a team that is completely lost. They have been in position to win several of these games and have simply failed to finish them.

They are close.

Now, they have to prove that being close can eventually turn into winning football games.

item.title: Cornerback Greg Newsome explains the Giants’ ballhawking ways
item.description: NY Giants cornerback Greg Newsome talks about the Giants’ mentality on defense.
item.content:encoded:
There were plenty of stories that came out of the New York Giants 36-24 win over the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4.

One of the biggest was how the Giants’ defense transformed itself after the Cardinals’ second drive. The story of the game has been how the Giants’ front seven took over the game, but the development of the secondary was just as important.

Veteran cornerback Greg Newsome II has been a steady presence on the outside for the Giants, and was one of three players to intercept Jacobi Brissett on Sunday. His experience and demeanor has led to him becoming one of the leaders on the back end of the Giants’ defense.

He was careful, though, to credit front seven players like Abdul Carter, Brian Burns, Tremaine Edmunds, and D.J. Reader.

“Guys are hunting,” Newsome said. “Guys are giving us chances to get our hands on footballs. It’s also great in the secondary that we’re playing tight coverage. We’re getting our heads around and just trying to find the football. But, like I said, once again, it’s rush and coverage working together, so without those guys up front, we wouldn’t have 14. Shout out to those guys up front.”

We anticipated before the season that Dennard Wilson would want to base his defense on “Step” coverage — that is, coverage with the cornerback within a step of the receiver. The philosophy is to challenge quarterbacks to consistently make tight window throws. Each of the Giants’ corners has upside in press-man coverage, and Newsome has been one of the best in the NFL in playing tight coverage.

The tight coverage combined with the pressure generated by the Giants’ front seven has the Giants among the league leaders in takeaways. The Giants are tied for third with eight total turnovers and tied for first in the NFL with six interceptions.

Newsome explained that the Giants’ secondary makes a point of practicing taking the ball away during the week.

“First, our coaches. Just how we structure practice,” he said. “We’re always doing takeaway things before we get into team activities and things like that. Obviously, I think our d-line, our front seven, the guys that are blitzing. I think they’re doing a great job of just pressuring the quarterback, affecting the quarterback, and just giving us a chance to make plays out there.”

It didn’t look so good to start the game against the Cardinals. The Giants’ defense made some plays, but were ultimately little more than a speedbump on the Cardinals’ first two drives. While the interior of the Giants’ defense was stout against Arizona’s runs, the perimeter proved vulnerable to well-schemed off-tackle runs.

The game was flipped on its head when Dennard Wilson began to call a much more aggressive defense and used the Giants’ speed to disrupt the Cardinals’ running game as well as their passing attack. That put the ball in Brissett’s hand and Brissett in less advantageous positions.

“Them stopping the run makes teams one-dimensional,” Newsome said. “It helps us out on the back end. It helps the linebackers not have to bite up on play fakes and things like that. I think with them doing such a great job up there with the front seven, it definitely helps our job, and just getting them on passing downs, allowing our guys to go up there and attack, so I think they’ve been doing an amazing job.”

This Giants team is playing with much more confidence and tenacity than fans are used to seeing from their squad. It shows in how they’ve won their last two games: Walk-off interceptions in the closing seconds of the game. However, John Harbaugh seems to be channeling Han Solo and is coaching his players to not let their confidence turn into cockiness.

“We’re underdogs every week, so that’s enough humbling for us,” Newsome said. “We’ve got to continue to keep going 1-0 each week. We don’t get too high, we don’t get too low. It’s a long season, so it’s great to be 3-1, but we have a lot of football left to play.”

Newsome mentioned “going 1-0”, which has been the message from the Giants’ front office and coaches. Observers noticed that the Giants’ brass was wearing tee shirts emblazoned with a “1-0” prior to Sunday’s game. The message is that the players need to focus on getting to a 1-0 record each week. The team seems to have bought into the mantra while they embrace the underdog mentality.

“I think we have a lot of vets in here that have played meaningful football that know how much each win matters,” Newsome said. “So we just focus on the next opponent. We don’t really care too much about the last game. It’s in the past, and now we’ve got to find a way to go 1-0 this week.”

The Giants have a 3-1 record and lead the NFC East, but you wouldn’t know it from how Newsome says the team is carrying itself.

“For sure you can play with an underdog mentality,” he said. “3-1 can easily turn into 3-14. That can easily do that. If you’re not careful enough, and if you have too much – if you’re not humble, you will get humbled. So, at the end of the day, we have to continue to have that mindset that we had in the beginning of the season, and we’re going to carry it the entire way. We definitely will keep that mindset.”

item.title: Kyle Juszczyk's $14,926 fine rescinded after 'juice box' explanation
item.description: Kyle Juszczyk was fined by the NFL for a celebration he did in Week 2. Here's why the league rescinded its fine before Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
The Juice was apparently not worth the squeeze.

San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle “Juice” Juszczyk will not have to pay the $14,926 fine imposed by the NFL after Week 2.

Juszczyk initially received the fine in response to the celebration he did after catching a touchdown pass against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, Sept. 20. The 14-year NFL veteran has used the juice drinking celebration often in his career, but the fine he received after Week 2 was the first one he received for doing it.

An NFL-NFLPA jointly appointed and compensated appeals officer reviewed Juszczyk's appeal, according to league spokesman Brian McCarthy. The appeals officer rescinded the fine after accepting the fullback's explanation: he was "simulating drinking a juice box."

Drink up 🧃

📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/t3IVHlapmi

— San Francisco 49ers (@49ers) September 20, 2026

According to Schefter's reporting last month, the NFL interpreted Juszczyk's Week 2 celebration as an "imitation of chugging a beer."

"Your imitation of chugging a beer constituted an offensive demonstration and could reasonably be construed as being in poor taste," the NFL wrote, per Schefter.

The ESPN insider also reported that Juszczyk had appealed the fine shortly after its imposition. The fullback said he doesn't brink beer.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Kyle Juszczyk's $14,926 fine rescinded after 'juice box' explanation
